#10041. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

#10040. Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in

Optional update fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2

A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again."

Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored."

Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

#10039. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. The session argued that most "AI for engineers" content focuses on individual productivity, while the real question for staff engineers is where their leverage comes from now. According to Cutler, AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where the leverage is.

The talk opened with a reflection on Cutler's previous conference talk, where he showed how AI could turn a four-hour task into four minutes. At that point he was shipping roughly as much as his whole team, which he described as multiplying himself rather than his team. That framed the central question of the session: what does a 10x engineer look like when everyone has AI?

To illustrate why this matters, Cutler shared internal Pinterest data on merged pull requests per engineer per week between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026. The top 10% of engineers went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per week, a 68% increase, while the bottom half went from 1.0 to 1.15, an increase of 14%. Everyone has AI, but not everyone uses it the same way, and the gap keeps growing. The presentation organized the response to that gap into three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.

The first move, multiply yourself, is about going first. Cutler explained that he tries new tools before his team does, and that part of that work is hitting dead ends so others don't have to. He mentioned examples such as an agent harness that could not be steered mid-task and a remote agent runner that required too many follow-ups. Sharing those findings early means the team does not lose a week on the same experiments. Running many agents also revealed a new problem: he kept giving the same corrections in every session, such as avoiding em-dashes, adding a diagram to the PR description, and keeping pull requests small.

The second move, multiply your team, started from a limitation: the folder made him faster, but only he had it. With new people joining the team and a new area to ramp up on, Cutler found himself repeating the same comments in code review, such as asking why a value is null instead of fixing the cause, testing like a user would, and keeping PRs small. The talk emphasized that the value of encoding that judgment grows with every teammate who adopts it, compared to the flat curve of a single engineer working alone.

The third move, multiply the system, is about moving up a level. Cutler used the history of container shipping as an analogy: ports got better at loading cargo by hand, but the standard box changed the economics entirely, from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo, one kind of change spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. Instead of running each migration by hand, the team built a system where a staff engineer points to a plan and an example, an engineer puts it on a schedule, and an agent running in a sandbox splits the work into PRs team by team. A class component migration ran three to five times faster than by hand, in the background while teams worked on other things.

The talk also covered what went wrong. One scheduled job looped and opened 16 PRs in two minutes, increasing CI wait times from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. The lesson was not to wait for the perfect guardrail, but to ship a small one. Cutler encouraged attendees to find their own "any" problem: a first responder for any incident, a draft fix for any bug ticket, or an agent that triages any flaky test. Today, 40 engineers have scheduler jobs of their own.

The results were significant. Using the same AI tools as other web teams, Cutler's team now ships about four times as much per engineer, without counting his own PRs.

The presentation concluded with practical steps: write down what you repeat, put it where people already work, and build for every case instead of one. Some parts of the job cannot be written down, like an honest conversation with a teammate who is struggling, and those remain the staff engineer's responsibility. As Cutler put it, a 10x engineer isn't ten times faster, they are the reason ten other people are. As AI agents become part of everyday development workflows, the role of senior engineers may increasingly shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into the tools, defaults, and systems that entire organizations use.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#10036. From Skiplists to B+ Trees: Making Valkey Sorted Sets More Memory Efficient

A sorted set can spend more memory describing how its elements are ordered than storing the elements themselves.

In Valkey 9.2 that changes: the skiplist is replaced by a high-fanout B+ tree variant called fbtree.

fbtree combines the high fanout and contiguous storage of a conventional B+ tree with several optimizations designed for Valkey's workload and memory allocator, including feature-based lookups, SIMD searches, linked leaves, and fast paths for sequential inserts and pops. In a 5-million-member test, it reduced per-member memory overhead by 36–43%, saving up to 109 MB.

Let's take a look at why this change happened and how it works.

Large sorted sets that exceed the listpack threshold are backed by a skiplist paired with a hashtable (smaller sorted sets use a compact listpack representation that stores elements sequentially in contiguous memory). The hashtable gives O(1) lookups by member, while the skiplist gives O(log n) ordered lookups by rank or score. That pairing is architecturally simple, but the skiplist carries a significant memory cost. It stores exactly one element per node, scattered across memory as separate allocations connected by pointers.

Valkey's skiplist pays for this in raw memory. Every node carries a backward pointer (8B), plus an average of 1.33 levels of forward pointers and span values, since skiplists are probabilistic (each node has a 25% chance of gaining another level). Each level costs 8B for the pointer plus 8B for the span value, giving around 29B of pointer and span overhead per node. Add the 8B score, and the total reaches roughly 37B per node before accounting for the member string.

Modern CPUs use a hierarchy of hardware caches (L1, L2, and L3) to keep frequently accessed data close to the processor. These caches are much smaller and faster than main memory (RAM), so when the CPU cannot find the data it needs in its cache, it must fetch it from a slower level of the memory hierarchy. As a rough illustration, an L1 cache hit can take about 1 ns, while a DRAM access can take around 100 ns. A dependent memory access can leave the core waiting; actual latency and how much work can be hidden vary by system and workload 1.

Each node in the skiplist is a separate allocation, potentially scattered wherever the heap happened to place it, so following the structure can require repeatedly fetching data from unrelated memory locations. Because each step can determine where the next step goes, these fetches are dependent, resulting in more round trips through the memory hierarchy. A 2025 study of concurrent in-memory indexes found that, on its tested workloads, traditional skiplists experienced roughly 2.4–4.8× more cache misses than a comparable B-tree, with 2–8× lower throughput 2 (testing different data structure implementations, not Valkey).

A B+ tree keeps entries sorted in fixed-size nodes: leaf nodes hold the entries, or pointers to them, and inner nodes hold just enough routing data to pick which child to descend into. Packing many entries into each node addresses both problems above: far less per-member pointer overhead, and far fewer dependent fetches per lookup.

fbtree, short for Feature B+ Tree, uses a 61-way fanout: each node can hold up to 61 entries or child pointers. Leaf and inner nodes are sized to fit jemalloc allocation classes without wasting space on 64-bit builds; on supported 32-bit builds, innerNode is rounded up to the 1280-byte class.

A 512-byte leaf holds up to 61 value pointers, so 61 members share one node instead of each getting its own. Instead of storing the score and member separately, fbtree stores them together as a single packed value: the normalized 8-byte score followed by the member bytes. This keeps the data needed for comparisons together and removes another level of pointer indirection.

The skiplist's 25%-per-level rule gives it an effective branching factor of about 4, while fbtree's fanout is 61. Both structures retain O(log n) search complexity, but the B+ tree has substantially fewer levels to traverse and therefore fewer opportunities for expensive memory fetches.

A modern CPU can also fetch several adjacent cache lines efficiently when the data is laid out contiguously, thanks in part to the way memory is accessed and to hardware prefetching 1. Therefore a B+ tree node that spans a few cache lines can be read efficiently as the CPU scans its contents.

On top of that structure, fbtree adds optimizations aimed at specific operations.

In a B+ tree keyed by variable-length strings, such as sorted set members, picking a child means comparing the lookup against each child’s anchor, the largest member in that child, and reading those strings costs memory fetches. fbtree's inner nodes store each anchor along with a small four-byte "feature." Because the anchors often share a common prefix, fbtree stores that shared prefix separately and uses the four feature bytes to distinguish the children. The implementation can then compare those features in parallel using SIMD, often identifying the correct child before fetching the child node itself. If the features uniquely identify a child, the search can descend immediately; otherwise, they still narrow the range that needs a full binary search.

Range commands such as ZRANGE walk the set in order. fbtree links its leaf nodes in a doubly-linked list, so a scan can move from leaf to leaf without climbing back up the tree. The skiplist requests an item, waits to receive it, and only knows the next item to fetch when it's received the first. The B+ tree can work on up to 61 items in parallel, and while it works on those it can fetch the next leaf node with the next 61 items.

Commands such as ZPOPMIN work at the ends of the set. fbtree caches its leftmost and rightmost leaves, so finding them is O(1), as in a skiplist, instead of O(log n). This keeps pop and append operations at parity rather than regressing.

Range deletions remove a contiguous run of members, and fbtree handles them without rebuilding the surrounding structure.

The change is internal: sorted set commands and their behavior remain unchanged. The one visible difference is that OBJECT ENCODING returns btree instead of skiplist for a large sorted set. If you have monitoring, tests, or tooling that checks for the literal string skiplist, that's one place to update. Small sorted sets under the listpack threshold are unaffected either way, since they never used the skiplist encoding to begin with.

The numbers below compare only the ordered index: skiplist versus fbtree, with the hashtable and member embedding unchanged.

Inserting 5 million 20-byte members sequentially reduced per-member memory overhead, excluding the member data itself, from 50.3B to 28.5B, a 43% reduction. The same 5 million members inserted in random order reduced per-member overhead from 50.3B to 32.0B, a 36% reduction.

The smaller reduction comes from random insertion leaving more partially filled nodes than sequential insertion.

For the 5-million-member set in this test, that is roughly 109 MB saved with sequential inserts and 92 MB with random inserts. The savings are per member, not per byte stored, so the relative reduction in total memory is largest for sets with many small members and shrinks as member size grows.

The benchmarks below were measured on PR #4206’s oi/pr3-fbtree-v2 branch and were not rerun for the merged commit. They were run on a Graviton3 c7g.metal system with 64 cores, nine I/O threads, a pipeline depth of 10, and a 3-million-member sorted set. Each test was repeated five times; the reported confidence intervals were ≤2% for all commands except ZRANDMEMBER.

The same underlying design changes also improve throughput for several sorted set operations:

ZADD and ZREM reposition elements in the tree, so they gain the most from fbtree's shallower structure and fewer pointer updates. Range operations see smaller gains because once the index traversal becomes cheap, producing and returning the requested elements becomes a larger part of the total cost. ZSCORE and ZRANDMEMBER barely move because they use the hashtable, not the ordered index.

The important takeaway: the commands didn't change, but in our tests large sorted sets carried 36–43% less per-member overhead, and ZADD and ZREM throughput rose 105% and 76%.

The goal wasn't simply to make the data structure faster in isolation: the implementation was repeatedly benchmarked against the existing skiplist through the full Valkey server, with optimizations added until fbtree matched or exceeded the skiplist across the tested sorted set commands.

Valkey 9.2 is currently in release-candidate testing. Before GA, try the 9.2 release candidate with your real workload, especially if large sorted sets or commands such as ZADD, ZREM, ZRANK, or ZCOUNT are important to you. Your testing and feedback can help surface issues before the final release, so open an issue with anything you find.

What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory

Bridging Cache-Friendliness and Concurrency: A Locality-Optimized In-Memory B-Skiplist

Rain Valentine is a software engineer at AWS working on Valkey's core data structures and performance. Her contributions include a B+ tree ordered index for sorted sets, improvements to the core hashtable, and more compact string storage — plus benchmarking and performance characterization across ARM, AMD, and Intel platforms. Rain skipped grad school partly to avoid writing papers and giving presentations, so it's kind of funny that people keep recruiting her for blog posts and putting her behind a podium.

#10035. Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand

Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.

The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.

The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.

The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.

The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.

In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US.

Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.

Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.

While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

"Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

"We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

"That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now."

The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.

The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users.

"A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data.

"Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

"Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies."

Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®
